samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are very close. Both explain the scan's limits, identify the div time slots as the blocker, fix them with radio buttons in a fieldset that show 'fully booked' in text, and add a role=status confirmation. B edges ahead because it says outright that removing the aria-labels lets speech and screen-reader users hear the visible words. Its code is also more complete: it includes CSS that hides the radios but keeps them focusable, moves focus to the time field when no time is chosen, and gives a readable confirmation instead of '19:00'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): The two answers are close: both correctly diagnose the div time slots, the hidden names that differ from the visible text, and the success shown only by a green border, and both offer nearly the same fix using native radio buttons and a live region. A edges ahead because it says the name mismatch affects both speech-control and screen-reader users, moves focus to the field on each validation error, and writes a readable confirmation ('6:00 pm' instead of '18:00'). B has a cleaner native form submit and a useful warning against display:none, but it doesn't say how the name mismatch affects screen-reader users and doesn't move focus when no time is chosen.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): The two answers are close. Both explain why the scan passes, identify the div slots as the blocker, flag the aria-label mismatches with WCAG 2.5.3, and replace the green-border-only feedback with a role=status message. A's code is a little stronger: it uses a real form submit, moves focus to the problem field for both errors, and its success message reads naturally ('6:00 pm' rather than '18:00'). A is also more accurate in saying aria-labelledby on a role-less div 'isn't reliably exposed'; B says it is simply ignored. Neither answer explicitly says the label mismatch also affects screen-reader users, only voice-control users. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): The two answers are close: both name the div time slots as the blocker, move to native radios, remove the mismatched aria-labels and add a status region that announces the result. A marks the full slot as 'fully booked' in visible text, as the rubric asks. B hides that text with sr-only, though B does add focus management on errors and a real form submit. A also separates the blocking problems from the smaller label mismatches more clearly, so it edges ahead on matching the rubric.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly identify the div slots as the blocker, recommend native radio inputs in a fieldset with 'fully booked' written as text, flag the label-in-name mismatches and add an announced confirmation. B ranks the problems more clearly as blockers versus other problems, and it also catches that the step is marked done before the request succeeds and handles booking failure. A's code includes the CSS and moves focus to the confirmation, but it assumes the user is on a Mac without any basis. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain the scan's limits, identify the div slots as the blocker, call out the label mismatches and propose a native radio group, so they are close. B's confirmation fix is more complete because it moves focus to the confirmation as well as announcing it, and it adds working CSS and a warning not to hide the inputs with display:none. A is tighter, separates blockers from other issues, and correctly marks the step done only after the request succeeds, with a failure message; B's unsupported 'since you're on a Mac' remark costs it a little on focus.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers open with a clear no and reject the claim that the script makes a site compliant or protects it from lawsuits, and both suggest testing the key flows by keyboard and screen reader and speaking to a lawyer. B is slightly fairer about the toolbar, calling it harmless as an extra courtesy feature. It also raises the risk of putting a third-party script on checkout pages and lists fixes specific to a shop, such as variant selectors. A is dismissive of the toolbar's value, but it does point out more directly that most fixes are made once per template, not separately on each of the sixty pages. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a clear 'don't buy it as the fix' verdict and explain well why overlays can't deliver compliance or legal protection. B fits the sixty-page shop better: it says most fixes happen at the template level rather than as sixty separate jobs, and it recommends seeing a lawyer about legal assurance in any case. A is somewhat fairer about the toolbar's value, calling it harmless as an extra, and it raises the third-party script risk. Even so, B's template focus and its questions for the sales rep make it slightly more practical.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a clear verdict, reject the compliance and lawsuit claims with the FTC example, and explain why an automatic script cannot fix alt text, labels, keyboard order or checkout. B is fairer about the toolbar: it calls the controls harmless and allows buying them as an extra convenience. A calls them mostly redundant and possibly harmful, without saying they help some visitors. A is slightly stronger on fixing at the template level, but B's balance and its clear split between the toolbar, the engine and the legal claim make it the better answer overall. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers open by saying not to buy it as a fix. Both reject the compliance and lawsuit promise, citing the FTC action against accessiBe, and both explain why automatic rewriting can't repair real barriers. A is somewhat fairer about the toolbar: it calls the toolbar harmless and allows buying it as an extra convenience, while B dismisses it as mostly redundant. B fits item 5 more closely: it explicitly recommends fixing problems at the template level for sixty pages, mentions the payment widget and gives a cost estimate for an audit. These strengths roughly cancel out.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a clear 'don't buy it as the fix' verdict and debunk the compliance and lawsuit promises well. B adds useful points: the script often can't reach checkout, it's extra third-party code, and the EAA applies to EU sales. A matches the rubric slightly better because it includes screen-reader testing in the owner's own checks and says the toolbar is fine as an extra once the real fixes are done. Neither gives much credit to the toolbar's real benefit for some visitors. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give the same clear verdict, question the legal promise and suggest a fix based on templates. B is fairer about the toolbar, calling it harmless and acceptable as an extra after the real fixes, where A mostly dismisses it. B also tells the user to test with a screen reader as well as a keyboard, naming VoiceOver and NVDA, which fits the template plan for sixty pages more closely.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same core problems: unlabeled percentages, a high-stakes send with locked content, owner chips that look settled, and no link from items to the transcript. B says outright that checking an item means leaving the screen and searching the transcript, and it suggests plain-language flags like "Check this." Its "what to keep" section is fuller and explains why each part should stay, though neither answer praises owner-next-to-task or the checkboxes. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover the core problems well: unexplained percentages, unreviewed sending, locked content and per-row transcript links. A states the verification cost more explicitly: the reader has to leave the screen and search the transcript. A also ties the 41% and 62% rows directly to the risk of the send, and its 'what to keep' section is fuller and explains why each part should stay. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the main case well: a large send button pushes unedited, model-written text and owners to every attendee, and nothing can be corrected in place. A wins because it explicitly calls out the false precision of the percentages, ties the summary to sources as well, and has a section on what works and should stay, which B leaves out entirely. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the main risk: unreviewed AI output goes to every attendee, with no way to edit text or owners in place. B covers more of the rubric. It names the false precision of the percentages, gives the summary a source link too, and has a 'What works' section that A lacks. A is thorough and has a useful priority order, but it says nothing about what to keep.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the unguarded send, the read-only text and owners, the unexplained percentages and the lack of per-row source links equally well. A goes further on false precision: it warns against showing raw numbers unless they are calibrated and suggests plain-word bands. However, A never says what works on the screen, while B has a clear 'What to keep' section. That section decides it for B. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers clearly flag the unguarded send to everyone, the lack of inline editing, and the need for per-row source links. B is stronger on the percentages: it questions whether they are calibrated and proposes plain-word bands instead. A balances its criticism with an explicit 'What to keep' section, which B mostly leaves out, and A is tighter overall.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers commit to inline edits as the main surface, keep a chat panel for open questions, and suggest a one-click way to apply chat output as a tracked change. B goes further on accountability: it calls an unreviewed silent change the worst failure, records which edits the model proposed and who accepted them, and offers a concrete test with a planted unrequested change. A is a little more concise, but neither answer says outright that the document must stay unchanged until the lawyer accepts an edit. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend inline edits as the main route and a chat panel for questions. Both also say clearly that copying across from the panel hides what changed and loses context. B ties its reasoning more directly to the lawyer's accountability for every word and is a bit more focused. A adds useful ideas, such as planting an unrequested change in a test, but runs longer. Neither answer says outright that proposed edits must never change the document before the lawyer accepts them, though both point that way through tracked changes and an audit trail.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers commit to inline suggestions as the main surface with chat as a secondary route, and both ground this in how lawyers redline, review diffs and stay accountable. Answer A edges ahead on item 3 because it explicitly keeps the assistant's changes separate from human ones and says pasted text loses its provenance. Answer B covers this only indirectly through attribution and an audit trail. Neither answer says outright that a proposed edit must not change the document until the lawyer accepts it. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers commit to inline edits as the main surface and keep chat as a secondary route, and both reason well from how lawyers redline. B does better on rubric item 3: it says the assistant's changes should stay distinct from human ones and notes that provenance is lost once text is pasted. A only mentions attribution in an audit trail, and neither answer says outright that edits must not change the document until the lawyer accepts them. B is slightly longer, with sections on testing and what it did not check, but it is still focused rather than a feature wishlist.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers recommend inline edits as the main surface with a panel for questions, reason from redlines and lawyer accountability, and suggest having the panel write its results back as inline suggestions. On item 3 each covers only half: A says AI-generated edits should be marked as such (provenance) but never says outright that edits must wait for acceptance, while B says 'never apply changes silently' but doesn't ask for AI-written text to be distinguishable. Both are about equally focused, with short lists of risks or design points and a modest suggestion to test with users. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers commit to inline editing as the main surface, keep a chat panel for open questions, and reason well from redlining, accountability and the cost of copying text across. B also requires AI-written edits to be marked so they can be told apart from counterparty and colleague changes, and it gives a sharper example of the main risk (a dropped 'not' or a changed defined term). A's 'never apply changes silently' covers acceptance but says nothing about provenance. Both are slightly long, B a little more so with its risks section and test plan.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers call the structure solid and handle the main problem well: the reset button looks the same as Save and sits right next to it. A then turns into an accessibility audit and raises some issues the markup doesn't support, such as the claim about screen readers and lowercase text and the touch-target concerns. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the real issue: the reset button looks like Save and sits next to it. A wins because it has fewer manufactured issues and ends by calling everything else polish. A labels its findings Blocker and Major, and one of them, 'no accessible names', is wrong because the markup has labels, as A itself admits later. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say 'mostly yes' and give the right reasons: about 8.5:1 contrast, a visible focus ring, a native button and a good size. B is a single sentence as requested, and its extra suggestions are hedged as optional ('could', 'if you ever animate it'), though it bundles two notes rather than one. A uses two sentences and calls its aria-label suggestion 'the one weakness', which reads less like an optional note. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say 'mostly yes' and give the same main reasons: about 8.5:1 contrast (my check gives about 8.2:1, still a pass), a visible focus ring, a native button and a comfortable size. A fits in one sentence as asked, but it adds two notes that aren't marked optional, and the reduced-motion one doesn't apply because the button has no animation. B uses two sentences, but its single note about a vague label when there are several buttons is relevant and conditional, so the strengths and weaknesses balance out.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A is closer to the one-line request: it is a single sentence, and its contrast figure is accurate (white on #1b4f8a is about 8.3:1). However, it hedges with 'mostly yes', calls the 'download receipt' label vague when it is reasonably descriptive, adds a note about a hypothetical icon, and never mentions that it's a native button. B uses three sentences, so it reads more like a small audit; it overstates the contrast (8.9:1), raises a hover concern only to dismiss it, and adds a touch-target check, though it does credit the native <button>. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B is closer to the one-line request: it is a single sentence, and its contrast estimate (about 8:1; the actual ratio is about 8.3:1) is accurate. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say yes with solid reasons, and each runs to two fairly dense sentences instead of one short line. B's contrast figure (about 8.3:1) is accurate. Its single note, that the #ffbf47 ring is only about 1.6:1 against a white page, is correct and points to a real weakness. A's note about repeated 'download receipt' labels is speculative, and neither answer marks its note as optional. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say 'mostly yes' in one long sentence that reads like a mini-audit, so neither is the short line the request asked for. A's numbers are more accurate (about 8.3:1 contrast, and the amber ring really is about 1.6:1 against white), but it presents the ring as a guideline failure that needs a fix rather than an optional note.
